sources.title: London Museum: Porter’s Badge from Smithfield Meat Market
sources.readScope: Object 78.75/2; description paragraphs on work roles, clothing and 1990s modernisation

excerpts.text: self-employed porters, who were paid according to how much they carried
blue overalls and white caps
automated steel rails

sources.contextParaphrase: The catalogue describes a green identification armband issued for 1977–78. Tenants were required to employ porters to move meat. Pullers back unloaded lorries, pitchers carried meat into the market, and a retailer paid a bummaree to remove a purchase. The City Corporation licensed porters. Modernisation in the mid-1990s moved carcasses on rails between climate-controlled storage and outside vehicles; a settlement ended the porters’ monopoly.
sources.limits: Historical catalogue synthesis, not an observed individual delivery. The adjective overhead is not supplied by this reopened passage.
sources.rights: Copyright not cleared for republication; short research excerpts and paraphrase only. No page or image bundled.

sources.title: London Museum: The history of Smithfield Market
sources.readScope: Sections on the covered market and A world of its own

excerpts.text: To give customers time to buy and prepare their meat for sale the same day
early houses

sources.contextParaphrase: The history explains why trade occurred at night: buyers needed time to prepare meat for sale that day. Workers finishing in the early morning could use pubs in or near the market that opened early for them. It also describes the nineteenth-century covered market. The end-of-day meaning of a morning drink in the script is an interpretive explanation of those hours.

sources.title: Heritage Gateway: Mountford House, 25 Britton Street
sources.readScope: Decision 18 April 2013; Summary, History and Details

excerpts.text: five Portland stone panels carved in low relief
just the right width for re-use there
split-level studio flats
too decayed to use

sources.contextParaphrase: The 1975–76 YRM building combined flats and offices and reused the 1901–03 E. W. Mountford facade of Booth’s Distillery offices from Turnmill Street. The assessment names Victor Kite and Brian Henderson. The facade matched the available width. First-floor studio flats were split level to accommodate its height. Decayed upper-floor and parapet Bath stone was renewed. F. W. Pomeroy’s five Portland-stone reliefs sit between second-floor windows. The building was assessed but not added to the national list.
sources.limits: No current foliage, sightline, pavement or individual panel-gesture inspection was made.
sources.rights: Copyright not cleared for republication; short research excerpts and paraphrase only. No page or image bundled.

sources.title: Survey of London, Volume 46: St John’s Gate and St John’s Lane
sources.readScope: Original 2008 chapter pp.142–163; PDF viewer pages 3 and 19 (zero-based 2 and 18); BHO capture saved 9 October 2024

excerpts.text: completed in 1504
an engraved view appearing on the title-page
painted on the doors of his coach

sources.contextParaphrase: The gate was completed in 1504 as the main entrance to the priory’s inner precinct. Cave had settled there by August 1730; the first Gentleman’s Magazine issue appeared in February 1731. Johnson worked for the magazine as contributor, translator and editor in the 1730s and 1740s. Cave used an image of the Gate on the magazine title page and on his coach doors in place of a coat of arms. The chapter also records earlier printing or publishing uses before Cave.
sources.limits: Historical scholarship and text reading only; present museum operation was not independently checked in this batch. Cave’s activity was not the Gate’s first publishing use.
sources.rights: Copyright not cleared for republication; short research excerpts and paraphrase only. No page or image bundled.

sources.title: James Boswell: Life of Johnson, volume I
sources.readScope: Early London account: Senate of Lilliput, Guthrie and Johnson’s debate reports; paragraphs beginning The debates in Parliament and These debates

excerpts.text: from the scanty notes furnished by persons employed to attend
Sometimes, however, as he himself told me
the part which they had taken

sources.contextParaphrase: Boswell says the disguised names could be deciphered. He attributes the earlier debate reports to Guthrie, who prepared remembered material before Johnson revised it. Later, Johnson composed reports from limited notes made by people attending both Houses. Boswell explicitly attributes to Johnson the recollection that, sometimes, he received only the speakers’ names and the side each took. This is a retrospective biographical account, not a claim that every report had no notes.
sources.limits: Preserve sometimes and the attributed recollection. Do not treat later editorial footnotes as contemporary testimony.
sources.rights: Historic text is public domain in many jurisdictions; this artifact still retains only short excerpts from the modern transcription.

sources.title: Samuel Johnson: Debates in the Senate of Lilliput, July 1741
sources.readScope: Opening heading, introductory paragraph and first speaker

excerpts.text: DEBATES in the SENATE of LILLIPUT
a parallel debate in the British Parliament
much desired by our readers
Hurgo Quadrert

sources.contextParaphrase: The transcription presents the July 1741 Gentleman’s Magazine text under its Lilliput heading. Its introduction explicitly connects the forthcoming report with readers’ desire for a parallel British parliamentary debate. The first speaker is Hurgo Quadrert. Modern bracketed identifications on the web page are editorial additions, not words attributed here to the original magazine.
sources.limits: Text transcription read; no original magazine scan inspected. The narrator’s interpretation of the disguise as a wink is interpretation.

sources.title: Survey of London, Volume 46: Clerkenwell Green
sources.readScope: Original 2008 chapter pp.86–114; PDF viewer page 51 (zero-based 50), paragraphs on 37A and Twentieth Century Press

excerpts.text: Under the management of Harry Quelch, editor of Justice
seventeen issues were printed here in 1902–3

sources.contextParaphrase: Twentieth Century Press occupied 37A from 1893 to publish Justice for the Social Democratic Federation. Quelch managed the press and edited Justice. Lenin was allowed to print Iskra there, and seventeen issues appeared in 1902–03. The press later expanded into adjacent premises. This locates the publishing operation and establishes the issue count and period.
sources.limits: Does not establish an unchanged modern office, furniture or visitor access.
sources.rights: Copyright not cleared for republication; short research excerpts and paraphrase only. No page or image bundled.

sources.title: V. I. Lenin: Harry Quelch
sources.readScope: 1913 obituary; paragraphs beginning Eleven years ago and Harry Quelch had; Collected Works vol.19 pp.369–371, George Hanna translation

excerpts.text: there was no room for another chair
by a thin partition
a very small writing-table, a bookshelf above it, and a chair

sources.contextParaphrase: Writing after Quelch’s death, Lenin recalls British Social Democrats headed by Quelch making their printing plant available to Iskra eleven years earlier. Quelch then occupied a partitioned corner. Lenin lists its small table, shelf and chair and says there was no space for a second chair when he visited. The story’s awkward visitor picture is an imaginative response to this recollection; no dialogue is documented.
sources.limits: Retrospective translated account, not a contemporaneous room survey. No claim of unchanged furniture.
sources.rights: Page states public domain, Marxists Internet Archive 2004; attribution retained. No image reproduced.

sources.title: London Museum: Rediscover London’s lost art of flower making
sources.readScope: 3 March 2016; Natasha Fenner / Beatrice Behlen interview; preparation, shaping and assembly paragraphs

excerpts.text: cutting tools
dye the fabric
special moulds
heat it over a spirit lamp
around the ball
twisted wire
paper or silk
sprays or wreaths

sources.contextParaphrase: The curator describes cutting fabric into petals with mallet-driven tools, dyeing it and drying it on porous paper. Moulds added veins. A rounded metal tool was heated over a spirit lamp and used to curve petals. Petals were assembled into flowers; twisted-wire stalks could be covered with paper or silk and combined into sprays or wreaths. The article connects artificial flowers to hats, bonnets and dresses and separately discusses John Groom’s work with disabled women. These are general trade processes, not an inventory observed at Woodbridge Chapel.
sources.limits: RES-006 applies: general technique must remain explicitly wider trade context. No evidence here that each named tool was in the chapel workroom.
sources.rights: Copyright not cleared for republication; short research excerpts and paraphrase only. No page or image bundled.

sources.title: Charles Booth inquiry notebook B237: mission interviews and Woodbridge visit
sources.readScope: Actual pixels inspected: canvas 116 manuscript p.117; canvas 123 p.131; canvas 161 p.207. Manifest retrieval failed; direct public image URLs succeeded.

excerpts.text: some 30 girls and women at work
schoolroom under the chapel
in process of enlargement
roses, daisies and cornflowers
After two years they become efficient

sources.contextParaphrase: Page 117 heads the Watercress and Flower Girls Christian Mission interview, names secretary John A. Groom and bears 11/5/98. The investigator says an assistant supplied information with Groom’s authority. Page 131 reports the training estimate. Page 207 records a later visit with Mr G. to Woodbridge Street: flower makers temporarily occupied the schoolroom while their usual room was enlarged. The count is approximate. The actual handwritten pages support the flowers named in the script. Page 207 itself was not assigned the earlier interview’s exact date.
sources.limits: Investigator identity not established. The two-year statement is an assistant’s reported estimate, not independently measured duration. No present-day imagery or physical access evidence.
